title: Trust broken
hookLine: abuses of power in some Western and Asian centers, and the communities that faced them

lines: A TEACHER ON A RAISED CUSHION.
cards: The teacher sits on a raised cushion at the front of the hall. Students bow when the teacher enters. The teacher's word on practice is final, and people have rearranged their lives to be near the teacher.
Often that trust is a gift; it lets a student go deep. But trust is also power, and power can be misused.
Today is uncomfortable, and it belongs in an honest course: what happened when trust was broken in some Buddhist communities, and what they did next.

teach.b: In some Buddhist centers, in Asia and in the West, teachers have misused the trust placed in them: sexual misconduct with students, bullying, money taken or hidden.
People who were harmed have described how hard it was to be heard, because the teacher was respected and the community wanted to protect its practice. Today is about what comes after someone speaks.
The Vinaya has a ceremony built for exactly that.

At the end of the rains retreat, each monk, the most senior first, faces the others and invites them: about anything they have seen, heard or suspected, speak to me, out of compassion, so I can make amends.
It's called the pavarana, the invitation. It takes for granted that anyone, however senior, may need correcting, and it puts that on the calendar. A second teaching is about how to speak.
To a prince named Abhaya, the Buddha says he won't say what is false or useless, however welcome.

teach.h: TRUE, USEFUL, AT THE RIGHT TIME.
teach.b: What is true and beneficial he will say even when it's unwelcome, and he knows the right time to say it. True, useful, timed with care. Communities that faced abuse have tried to build both into their life.
They listened to the people who were harmed, and took them seriously enough to look. They brought in outside investigators. Some teachers stepped down.
Groups wrote ethics codes, named people other than the teacher to receive concerns, and went to the police when a crime was involved. None of it undoes the harm.
But it can make the room safer for the next student.

how: Some Buddhist centers now publish ethics codes, name contacts outside the teacher for raising concerns, and ask outside investigators to look into complaints; Theravada monastic communities hold the pavarana at the end of the rains retreat, inviting one another to point out faults.

practice: Think of a group you belong to, a center, a congregation, a team, and ask quietly: if something were wrong here, who would I tell besides the person in charge, and is there a written way?
If you don't know, notice that without alarm. If someone comes to mind who might need help right now, breathe with that, and know that a trusted person or the local authorities can be called.

wordCard.voice: Trust broken. When teachers in some Buddhist communities misused their power, and the communities learned to listen, investigate and make things safer. Today's word.
